First, looking at option 1: "شمشیر نیک از آهن بد چون کند کسی؟ - ناکس تربیت نشود ای حکیم کس". Translating this, it's something like "A good sword made from bad iron, how can it be made by someone? - A bad person cannot be educated, O wise one." So this is saying that a good outcome (a good sword) can't come from a bad material (bad iron), implying that bad people can't be reformed. The message is about the inherent qualities of a person or object determining their outcome.

Option 2: "سگ به دریای هفت گانه بشوی - که چو تر شد پلیدتر باشد". Translating: "A dog goes to the seven seas - which when it becomes a dog, it becomes more impure." Wait, maybe the second line is "which when it becomes a dog, it becomes more impure"? Or maybe "when it becomes a dog, it becomes more impure"? Hmm, that seems a bit confusing. Maybe it's saying that if a dog (which is already impure) goes to the seven seas (a place of purity or transformation?), it becomes even more impure. Or perhaps the structure is different. Alternatively, maybe the second line is "which when it becomes a dog, it becomes more impure." But that doesn't make much sense. Wait, maybe the first line is "A dog goes to the seven seas" and the second line is "when it becomes a dog, it becomes more impure." That seems contradictory. Maybe the translation is off. Alternatively, maybe it's about a dog being immersed in the seven seas (a metaphor for a lot of things) and then becoming more impure. The message here might be that even if you put something impure in a pure environment, it remains impure or becomes worse. So similar to option 1, which is about bad people not being able to be educated.

Option 3: "ز وحشی نیاید که مردم شود - به سعی اندر او تربیت گم شود". Translating: "A wild beast does not come to be a human - in trying to educate it, you lose your teaching." This seems to be saying that a wild animal can't become a human, and trying to educate it is a waste. So again, the idea that something inherently wild or bad can't be transformed into something good through education. Similar to option 1 and 2.

Option 4: "سگ اصحاب کهف روزی چند - پی نیکان گرفت و مردم شد". Translating: "The dog of the cave dwellers (people in the cave) for several days - took the path of the righteous and became a human." Wait, "سگ اصحاب کهف" might refer to the dog of the people of the cave, which is a reference to the story of the Companions of the Cave (from the Quran, Surah Al-Kahf). In that story, the dog is mentioned as being with them. The second line says "took the path of the righteous and became a human." That seems different because it's about a dog (which is an animal) becoming a human through following the righteous path. So this one is about transformation from an animal to a human through good deeds, which is the opposite of the other options where bad things can't be transformed into good.

So options 1, 2, and 3 all talk about how bad or impure things can't be changed into good through education or effort. Option 4 is about a dog (animal) becoming a human (good) by following the righteous path. Therefore, option 4 is the outlier because it's the only one that suggests transformation from bad to good, while the others say that bad can't be turned into good.
